parole.testo: Uncertain. Most Romanists conclude that the word ultimately comes from Latin coactāre, but they are uncertain how exactly it evolved due to phonological problems and the early attestation in Portuguese and Galician. It could possibly be: * From Spanish agachar; * From an unattested Vulgar Latin *coa

parole.significato: any of several grubs and beetles that bore through wood or books, or that infest grain
parole.testo: Unknown. Maybe from Latin carbunculus. If so, it is a doublet of carbúnculo. Alternative theories include derivation from Latin cariēs or caruncula. Possibly entered Portuguese via Spanish caroncho.
Ultimately from Latin cornus, probably through Spanish cornizo < Vulgar Latin *corniceus.

parole.significato: to push (apply a force to an object so that it moves away)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *enpurrar (attested as the hapax derived term enpurron); further etymology is uncertain. parole.significato: mildew (growth of minute fungi on plants)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“blemish”), probably via Spanish mangla. Doublet of mancha, malha, mágoa, mácula, and maquis.

Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *palātārem, derived from Latin palātum. Considering its intervocalic /l/, presumably borrowed via Spanish paladar. Doublet of padar (the inherited counterpart); cf. also Galician padal.

parole.significato: shoot or stem of a vine with leaves
parole.testo: From Latin pampinus, possibly by way of Spanish pámpano; compare Galician pampo, showing inherited loss of intervocalic 'n'. Compare also Sicilian pàmpina.

parole.significato: common sense (the ability to make good judgements based on reason)
parole.testo: Uncertain origin. Possible origins include: * from Latin tenus; * from Latin tenue; * from Spanish tino, of uncertain origin.
